title: How Matt Pocock fixes the PR bottleneck: automated checks, automated review, then lighter human review
summary: Matt argues AI-driven PR volume needs "brakes" so a software factory doesn't become a slop cannon. He layers cheap automated checks, a separate coding-standards reviewer agent that commits fixes, and a human-friendly PR (merge danger, diagrams, retro) so human review gets faster.

principles.text: Layer automated checks, automated review, and human review so human review gets faster, not skipped.
principles.quote: the goal here is to make human review faster by leaning on those first two phases.

principles.text: Checks are cheap, so add many, but a green CI can lie; review layers exist to detect those lies.
principles.quote: Does a green CI mean that the code is ready for merge? No, it does not.

principles.text: Tautological and structure-sensitive tests restate the implementation and break on any rename or refactor.
principles.quote: They're very sensitive to the actual internal workings of the system.

principles.text: Design deep modules (simple interface, big hidden implementation) so agents test at the interface, not internals.
principles.quote: you're going to have fewer structure sensitive tests because you're hiding more of the implementation behind that interface.

principles.text: Keep coding standards out of the overloaded implementer; enforce them in a separate review subagent that commits fixes.
principles.quote: don't put coding standards in your implementer agent.

principles.text: Treat the process producing code as reviewable too: never write the same review comment twice, use a retro to compound.
principles.quote: you never want to write the same comment twice.
